item.title: Economic pressures put new Midwestern states in play for the midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Supporters listen as Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a rally at Wayne State University in Detroit on October 22. - Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images Democrats could be poised for a revival in the heartland, as furor over high costs and doubt about President Donald Trump’s willingness to change the nation’s trajectory threaten to loosen the GOP’s grip on working-class voters. A decade after the Trump era began, when he first turned Midwestern political battlegrounds into reliably Republican states, the fallout from policies of his second term have rippled through the agriculture sector and broader economies across the Great Plains and the Rust Belt. Iowa and Ohio, which have not been competitive since former President Barack Obama was on the ballot, are in play. And ruby-red states like Kansas, Nebraska and Indiana are not exempt. The shift is happening up and down the ballot, with tight contests for the House, Senate and governor blanketing the middle of the country. From spring planting to fall harvest, anxiety over Trump’s war with Iran and the fallout from his trade battles has turned into alarm. In conversations across the region, voters point to the soaring cost of gas and diesel , as well as high grocery prices and interest rates. A whipsaw tariff policy has forced farmers to pay more for fertilizer, while some manufacturers, footing higher bills for imported components, have laid off workers. Trump’s decision to allow imported beef has infuriated ranchers. And spending cuts targeting healthcare and grant programs have caused further strain. Promises to revitalize the nation’s manufacturing sector remain unfulfilled. And even before the Iran war sent costs soaring, several of these battleground states were in fiscal decline. Iowa, for example, recorded the weakest annual growth rate in the country in 2025, according to the federal Bureau of Economic Analysis, a searing indictment for Republicans who have had control of state government for more than a decade. “I think everybody in agriculture is tired, would be the best way to put it. They’re just tired,” Steve Kuiper, a farmer and president of the Iowa Corn Growers Association, told CNN. “They feel very beat up right now, demoralized.” It has all fueled a hunger for change — and created an opening for Democratic candidates. “A lot of the promises the president made to bring costs down, to not start new foreign wars, to deliver on his economic message, have not come to fruition,” said Beau Bayh, the third-generation scion of Indiana’s most famous Democratic political family. If he wins his race for secretary of state, he’d be the first member of his party to win statewide in Indiana in 14 years. Trump knows better than most presidents that midterm elections are a reflection — and referendum — on the party in power. He experienced it in 2018, when Republicans held control of the Senate but lost their majority in the House — including three seats in Iowa. GOP officials tell CNN they fear a repeat of that scenario. The US Capitol building seen on October 1 in Washington, DC. - Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images The travel plans of both parties tell the tale, with Trump set to visit Michigan on Sunday after making stops in Ohio, Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa in a monthlong campaign blitz. Obama traveled to Michigan and Ohio on Saturday, rallying support in two states he once won. Polls suggest voters are willing to punish the Republicans in power in Washington, even though they also hold dim views of the Democratic brand. “It’s not that they’ve been overwhelmed by the Democratic Party, it’s just that they’re really, really pissed off,” Tom Vilsack, a Democratic former Iowa governor, told CNN. “They want to send a message of disappointment. When you’re upset with someone, you want to find a way to send a message. You don’t swallow it, you send that message.” Vilsack, who served two terms as agriculture secretary in the Obama administration, said economic frustrations across the agriculture and manufacturing sectors have been rising long before the Trump era. But he said the promises Trump made during his three campaigns, particularly when he pledged to bring prices down only two years ago, are feeding the anger. “He builds up the hope that it’s going to be fundamentally different,” Vilsack said. “That was interpreted that he’s going to bring back the good times. He failed to do that.” Former Minnesota Gov. Tim Pawlenty, who was the last Republican to win that office in his reelection two decades ago, said Trump would be better off talking about rising costs and how he intends to change course. “It’s going to be a blue wave,” Pawlenty told CNN. “We just don’t know if it’s knee-deep, waist-deep, or going to hit us right in the face.” The House is all but certain to fall from GOP control, he said, but added: “The real chance for Republicans to salvage something out of this is to hang on to the Senate and that’s a real possibility.” House and Senate in the balance In Iowa and Ohio, Democrats have a shot at winning Senate races that are crucial to the net four-seat gain they need to claim a majority — a goal that eluded them in 2018. Their odds look even better in those states’ governor’s races, potentially giving the party a foothold in statehouses where Republicans have trifectas: control of the executive, legislative and judicial branches. But the Democratic revival could extend even further. Megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton has the GOP scrambling to save the seat of Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas . An independent candidate, Dan Osborn, has rallied Democratic support and thrown a curveball into Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts’ bid for a second term in Nebraska. And a slew of House seats across the Midwest held by Republicans are in play. Democrats believe they could win as many as three GOP-held seats each in Iowa and Ohio, plus potentially four more in Michigan. The party is also targeting an Omaha-based district in Nebraska and one in southeastern Wisconsin’s Driftless Area. If the election breaks in Democrats’ favor in a big way, another House seat in Nebraska, as well as one seat each in Indiana and Kansas, could also prove to be much more competitive than either party expected early in the 2026 election cycle. Republicans aren’t conceding any of those races. And they believe they have Democrats on defense in the Upper Midwest — particularly Michigan, where progressive former public health official Abdul El-Sayed is locked in an expensive and bitter Senate race against Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers. unknown content item - Speaking in Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday, Trump urged voters to pretend he was on the ballot and vote to ensure a “booming Iowa economy.” “If you get out and vote like you did in 2024, we win in a landslide, you know, we win in a landslide,” he said Even as the president boasts of America’s golden age, with an economy envied by the world, he also makes clear he understands the challenges people are facing. At most every stop along the way of his red-state October blitz, he has offered sweeteners to voters if they stick with Republican candidates. From $8 billion in new aid to farmers announced in Kansas to promises of building the nation’s largest steel plant in eastern Iowa to a commitment he made in Nebraska to temporarily ease diesel costs, Trump has made a series of pledges that follow his offer of giving every adult American $5,000 if Republicans retain their grip on Washington. The promises are barely even repeated by GOP candidates, who know they ring hollow with many voters. Democrats acknowledge the uphill climb for winning all of the narrowly divided Senate races across the Midwest, particularly given their own brand and favorability challenges. But Republican officials wonder whether Trump’s extensive travels to many of these states will backfire on down-ballot races. “When our leader, the president himself, does things that make me cringe, that’s difficult to tell people to vote for me,” said Jim Howell, a Republican member of the Sedgwick County Board of Commissioners in Wichita, who is also on the November ballot. “I really wish we had leaders that don’t make us cringe, but help us consider a way to come together.” Trump’s closing message A question hanging over the final week of the race is whether Trump’s relentless campaigning has awakened Republican voters to rally to his aid one last time in hopes of closing an enthusiasm gap. Iowa could be a place to watch, given Trump’s long history of winning there and his decision to hold two rallies in opposite corners of the state in the homestretch. But the president’s approach, a little more than one week from Election Day, has been to double down on the policies that have led many voters to sour on his second term. In Trump’s Sunday trip to Michigan, he’ll hold a rally at Port Huron — on the Canadian border. It will put on display his tariff battle with the United States’ northern neighbor, even though the party’s Senate nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has attempted to break with Trump over the tariffs. “Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war — now,” Rogers said in a television ad his campaign launched this month. The GOP’s best hope might be to lean into the cultural battles that have helped them win over White, rural, working-class voters in recent elections. In Michigan, both Trump and Rogers have attempted to brand the Democratic nominee, El-Sayed, as supportive of extremist Islamist interests. But Democrats are fighting back. El-Sayed in recent days began airing an ad that features clips of Republicans and conservative media figures, including Fox News hosts, saying nice or helpful things about him and his campaign. Before those clips play, he lists issues where he suggests common cause with some in the MAGA movement, such as releasing the Jeffrey Epstein files and combatting Washington corruption. Ohio is another headache for Republicans. The party’s nominee for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, faced sharp criticism from the man he is running to replace, two-term GOP Gov. Mike DeWine, for airing a controversial advertisement featuring the mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton. Gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, alongside US President Donald Trump, speaks in Youngstown, Ohio, on October 12. - Kevin Lamarque/Reuters Both Ramaswamy and the president have dug in, defending the ad — and in doing so have turned the race into a test of whether voters will accept Trumpian tactics from candidates who are not Trump. And what’s receded from the forefront is the issue Ohio voters who spoke with CNN in recent days — including Republicans who support Ramaswamy — said is responsible for the state’s sudden competitiveness: the cost of living. “We all have to get gas. I have to go get gas right now in my car, and that’s difficult,” said Sheri Vorherr, a 55-year-old mother of five from Loveland who volunteered at a Ramaswamy rally in Cincinnati on Wednesday. She said she helps her oldest daughter buy groceries each week and sees the economic pinch brought on by inflation. “I don’t think it’s an easy fix. I think it’s things that are going to take time,” she said. “I do believe Trump is trying to do that — it’s just taking a lot longer.” CNN’s Phil Mattingly contributed to this report. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/25/politics/midwest-midterm-elections-michigan-ohio-iowa

item.title: Brazil's tight runoff tests Trump officials' bid to bring Bolsonaros back to power
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Gabriel Stargardter SAO PAULO, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Two US State Department officials led a campaign to restore the right-wing Bolsonaro clan to power in Brazil and successfully pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor, according to 10 current and former US officials with direct knowledge of the matter. Their plan faces a reckoning on Sunday, when Senator Flavio Bolsonaro faces leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight run-off. Lula has warned Washington against encroaching on Brazil's sovereignty and accused his opponent of plotting with the Trump administration. The two officials were Darren Beattie, a Senior Advisor ‌for Western Hemisphere Affairs who oversees Brazil policy, and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor promoted this year to Deputy Assistant Secretary for North America. The details of their campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power haven't been previously reported. Beattie and Pita, both political appointees, operated with wide latitude to manage Washington's relationship with the ‌second most-populous country in the Americas, the people said. In the months before election campaigning began, they instructed US diplomats in Brazil that it was US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader – even though he had been disqualified from office for plotting a coup in 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula, three of the people said. After Bolsonaro received a 27-year sentence in September 2025, the two men pivoted to ​supporting the candidacy of his son, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the three sources said. Beattie and Pita told embassy staff not to interact with other conservative presidential contenders who could challenge the younger Bolsonaro, they said. Since last year, the two men have successfully advocated for punitive US government measures on Brazil designed to weaken Lula and boost the Bolsonaros, the 10 people told Reuters. The policies included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and imposing US sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who was spearheading the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro. Reuters could not determine the extent to which the two men were acting on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump, a vocal defender of Bolsonaro since his election defeat in 2022, hasn’t publicly endorsed any candidate. The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the State Department. State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott didn't answer questions about specific measures and directives involving Beattie and Pita but said in a statement: "All actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to ‌choose their leaders through free and fair elections." Lula’s office did not respond to comment requests. Orna Blum, one of the officials who ⁠spoke to Reuters about Beattie and Pita’s efforts, led the State Department's Brazil and Southern Cone office until retiring last year over her opposition to the Trump administration. Washington "has every right to pursue its economic and strategic interests," she said. "But when American foreign policy instruments are used to pressure another democracy over the legal fate of a political ally, the line between diplomacy and political intervention has been crossed." SANCTIONS ON A SUPREME COURT JUSTICE Beattie is a former White House speechwriter fired in 2018 after addressing an event frequented by white nationalists. He’s also the architect of "free speech ⁠diplomacy," a policy advocated by Trump allies that seeks to punish nations they accuse of censoring right-wing speech by US citizens, companies and global right-wing allies. The United States has accused Brazil Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of violating free speech rights by jailing Brazilians for political social-media posts and by censoring content of US social-media companies. Moraes has argued he was ridding social media of fake news that undermined public faith in Brazil's democratic institutions. Moraes did not respond to a comment request. Pita, a conservative Venezuelan-American, is among many in Rubio's orbit who view Lula as a threat to US interests in Latin America. Rubio has been a key leader in the administration’s aggressive policy in the region, which has included an invasion of Venezuela to oust its president, an oil blockade of Cuba, and military attacks ​on suspected ​drug boats from Latin America. Beattie and Pita were drawn to the Bolsonaro family’s right-wing politics, their antipathy towards Lula, and the idea that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of abuses by Brazil's Supreme Court. Like ​Trump in the 2020 US election, Bolsonaro refused to concede he lost Brazil’s 2022 presidential vote, triggering riots by supporters who stormed government ‌buildings. The Supreme Court convicted him in September 2025 of plotting a coup to remain in power. Before the conviction, in early 2025, the Bolsonaros were aggressively lobbying Washington for sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act against Moraes, who had led criminal investigations into Jair Bolsonaro. The act is a 2016 federal law allowing US sanctions against foreign individuals responsible for human-rights abuses or severe corruption. Around April 2025, Jair Bolsonaro’s younger son, Eduardo, visited Beattie in his State Department office in Washington DC, according to two former US officials. Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was "practically certain" the Trump administration would do so. Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment. Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said. The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts. A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are "fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy." TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil's top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, ‌who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime. Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups. In May 2025, ​Pita joined a US delegation that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions ​official at the time. Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those announced against Mexican cartels in February 2025 could be used ​in Brazil, one former official said. Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss "the urgency of designating the ‌PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations," according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included ​photos of the attendees. The State Department announced the designation the following day. Reuters could not determine the ​extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision. BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices' visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the "persecution" of Jair Bolsonaro. Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil. Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro's trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government's poll numbers, the analysts said. Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including ​meatpacking giant JBS - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down. Beattie ‌and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March Brazil barred Beattie from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison. Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, ​said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil's election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity. Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory. "Close, but a very, very ​big victory," he told reporters. "Amazing, actually." (Reporting by Gabriel StargardterAdditional reporting by Gram Slattery in Washington, Luciana Magalhaes in Sao Paulo, Lisandra Paraguassu in Brasilia Editing by Brad Haynes and Richard Valdmanis) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/inside-trump-administration-campaign-return-214506018.html

item.title: Inflation under Trump is only about half the rate under Biden. Voters are still just as mad.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
So far in President Trump's second term, prices in the US have risen only about half as quickly compared to his predecessor's four years in office. Yet Trump has a 72% disapproval rating on the issue and risks paying a steep political price — just as former President Joe Biden did — with voters drawing a direct connection between rising prices and the president's policies. In the last election cycle, prices of all items rose more than 20% during Biden's term , sparking widespread voter angst. This time around, price growth is notably slower, rising 5.4% in a little less than two years since Inauguration Day. But a Yahoo Finance analysis of price data shows that a few major outliers have hit Americans' wallets in an outsized way, largely due to increases in goods affected by the war in Iran and tariffs. Fuel oil and gasoline are perhaps the most dramatic examples, spiking over 30% beginning in March in response to the war in Iran and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz. And voters have noticed, as evidenced in poll after poll. A New York Times/Siena poll released this week found 73% of likely voters disapprove of the president's handling of gas prices. Trump underscored the salience of energy prices when he posted a charge this week that "Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the US Midterm Election." Trump has often pushed back against questions about high energy prices, saying they won't be a problem once the Iran war ends. Read more: How oil price shocks ripple through your wallet, from gas to groceries Link between price spikes and Trump policies The connection between price increases and Trump's tariff policy has also been in evidence. Coffee prices have risen nearly 23% during Trump's second term (more than double the rate under Biden) as tariffs raised prices before Trump scrapped many of the coffee duties late last year in response to coffee drinkers' unhappiness. Goods like toys and footwear have likewise risen rapidly as importers from China and elsewhere in Asia faced new tariffs. Toys are a particularly stark example, falling by 4.6% during Biden's term and then rising by 7.8% so far in Trump's term. "Maybe the children will have two dolls instead of 30 dolls, and maybe the two dolls will cost a couple of bucks more than they would normally," Trump said in a rare acknowledgment of tariff-fueled price increases when he was pressed on the issue in April. Other goods have moved in the opposite direction. Eggs jumped by an average of 2.57% each month when Biden was in the White House, but have dropped 3.82% each month of Trump's term so far, the analysis shows. But tariffs remain in focus and unpopular, with an average of polls from the Silver Bulletin finding that 62.7% of Americans disapprove of how Trump has handled trade and tariffs versus 32.8% who approve. President Donald Trump is seen after a rally on October 22 in Sioux City, Iowa.. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images) Anna Moneymaker via Getty Images Gas in focus in the final weeks of the campaign Despite the different roots, inflation has emerged as the central political problem for Trump and his party — as it was for Biden and Democrats — and comes as early voting is already underway for the Nov. 3 midterms. And perhaps no individual price tag is more politically charged, for any president, than the cost of a gallon of gas. Trump is trying to make his case as gas prices are averaging about $4.30 per gallon and diesel is elevated after setting an all-time price record last month, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). Trump has taken multiple actions just this week to try to rein in prices, including $8 billion in support for farmers and invoking the Defense Production Act on Thursday to direct new funds to increase refining capacity. Yahoo Finance Trump touted the moves before voters in Iowa on Thursday , saying the release of $150 million would lead to more production of diesel and gasoline. Yet he faces the inconvenient fact that his record on gas prices is now all but indistinguishable from Biden's. Since Jan. 20, 2025, prices have averaged $3.449 per gallon according to data from the Energy Information Administration . Under Biden, the average price was $3.455 per gallon over his four years. Trump spent much of the last campaign promising the opposite, pledging $ 2 per gallon gasoline and vanishing inflation in nearly every 2024 campaign speech. That is leading voters to blame the president for the state of affairs. This week's national poll from the New York Times and Siena University found that 75% of voters view economic conditions as only fair or poor, and a solid majority put the blame on Trump. As Ipsos also put it this week in a summary of recent findings : "Americans' confidence in the economy has been bad since the Iran war began [and] now the bottom has dropped out." Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. This article originally appeared on Yahoo Finance at https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article/inflation-under-trump-is-only-about-half-the-rate-under-biden-voters-are-still-just-as-mad-120043933.html

item.title: Amy Acton urges Trump and Vance to 'look at the facts' after Ramaswamy attack ad
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Ohio Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton told ABC News in an interview Saturday that she hopes President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance will "look at the facts" of the abuse she says she endured as a child after they defended an attack ad made by GOP nominee Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign. Bipartisan backlash has hit Ramaswamy's campaign, after the release of the ad featuring Acton's estranged mother who Acton says stood by the man who was criminally charged with sexually abusing her as a child. Acton said she hasn't seen her mother since she was 12 years old. In the ad, Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, said Acton has lied about her past, though it doesn't mention the allegations of sexual abuse. Sue Ogrocki/AP Photo - PHOTO: Amy Acton In response to Trump and Vance who have doubled down on and defended the ad, Acton told ABC News, "My job is to work with anyone on any side of the aisle to solve problems instead of making them, and I would say I do hope they would look at the facts." Acton spoke to ABC News after a rally in Cleveland with former President Barack Obama. Trump doubles down on Amy Acton criticism as Ramaswamy ad controversy swirls Acton has alleged her mother's second husband molested her between the ages of 9 and 12. Charges were filed against her stepfather, and Acton testified against him. He pleaded not guilty, but fled the state before trial and never appeared before a judge. He died in 2004. Shannon Stapleton/Reuters - PHOTO: Ohio Midterm Elections Acton said she and her brother endured "extreme child abuse and neglect" in their childhood. "We were frequent flyers in children's services ... There are facts in this case: a grand jury indictment, fugitive out against bail, and that behavior went on and on," Acton said. Speaking to reporters this week about the ad, Trump dismissed questions about the allegations of Acton's sexual abuse, asserting at multiple points that the ad has "nothing to do" with Acton's stepfather. Spencer Platt/Getty Images - PHOTO: Ohio Republican Candidates Campaign At The Circleville Pumpkin Show Rally Similarly, Vance told rally attendees in Ohio earlier this week that he is "a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America." GOP Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, who on Thursday told reporters in Columbus, Ohio, that the ad is "deeply, deeply troubling" and that the Ramaswamy campaign "needs to take it down," but he did not withdraw his endorsement of Ramaswamy. Asked whether she was disappointed that DeWine didn't withdraw his endorsement, Acton said it was "an honor and a privilege" to work with him during COVID-19 pandemic as the director of the Ohio Department of Health. Vance praises Ramaswamy for having 'audacity' to run controversial Amy Acton ad "I really do appreciate him calling out the facts of the case," Acton said. "That this was an indictment he knows better than others. He's a prosecutor. He started his career prosecuting cases like this, and he knew more than anyone. He knows who I am and knows my story." Speaking to reporters on Friday, Ramaswamy said the ad had nothing to do with childhood abuse. "We ran an ad about lying," he said. "Amy Acton is lying. She has been lying this entire campaign about me, about her record, about her history in this state." In a statement to ABC News, Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy said: "Ohioans can't afford a liberal governor who shows up for Obama but never shows up for them." Ramaswamy and Acton have never met in person. Asked what she would say to him, Acton said: "I really have no words for Mr. Ramaswamy. I think there is no low that he wouldn't sink to." Speaking to survivors of abuse, Acton said: "For those out there going through it now, hold on, please. If there's someone you feel safe with, say something about it." Obama blasts Trump, says Ramaswamy 'thirsty' for attention Acton campaigned Saturday alongside former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who's running to win back his seat, and Obama, who was the last Democratic presidential candidate to win the state of Ohio in a presidential election in 2012. Sue Ogrocki/AP Photo - PHOTO: Amy Acton,Barack Obama,Sherrod Brown Democrats are eyeing the Senate and gubernatorial races as key pickup opportunities given the headwinds facing Republicans. Amy Acton campaign slams Ramaswamy over controversial ad featuring estranged mother In his remarks, Obama delivered a scathing rebuke of the Trump administration on a variety of issues — from the economy to immigration to the war in Iran. Regarding the GOP candidate for governor, Obama called Ramaswamy "thirsty" for attention. Sue Ogrocki/AP Photo - PHOTO: Election 2026 Ohio Senate "Vivek's own supporters know it's all about what's in it for him," Obama said. "We all know that guy, you know, who ... just wants to get attention no matter what, willing to do anything. And in recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to." Obama emphasized what he called a "moral component" to this election and said that "basic decency" is missing from the current public discourse. ABC News' Diana Paulsen contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/amy-acton-trump-vance-facts-abuse-after-ramaswamy/story?id=137543717

item.title: 'Weaponizing the law': California AG slams DOJ's attack on alleged noncitizen voting
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
People cast their ballots at St Mary's Episcopal church during the first day of early voting in Los Angeles, California, on Saturday. Photograph: Chris Torres/EPA California’s attorney general on Saturday rebuked the Trump administration’s efforts to quash alleged noncitizen voting, calling it “politicizing and weaponizing the law”. Rob Bonta, the state’s attorney general, said the justice department acted at Donald Trump’s direction. “It is once again the United States Department of Justice politicizing and weaponizing the law to attack its enemies, and it is completely improper,” he told MS Now. Less than two weeks before the midterms, federal prosecutors called upon California election officials to verify within 48 hours a list of about 20,000 ballots belonging to suspected noncitizens. Noncitizen voting is extremely rare , but in the run-up to the midterm elections, the justice department has ramped up prosecutions of people accused of illegally voting while not holding US citizenship. California’s election personnel have raised concern that the administration’s directive could disenfranchise citizens. Los Angeles officials said this week a “high percentage” of the individuals on the list were born in the United States. “Trump’s DOJ is so desperate to invent ‘widespread voter fraud,’ it sent California counties lists of people who NEVER voted – and voters from the WRONG COUNTY. Absolute clown show!” California’s governor Gavin Newsom posted on social media . “Voter intimidation has no place in our democracy,” Pete Aguilar, a congressman representing south-west San Bernardino county, said in a social media post . The federal government’s oversight attempts come amid a national Republican effort to crack down on alleged voter fraud, particularly any cases among undocumented immigrants. “We are asking each county election official to commit to working with us by providing the necessary information for DHS to quickly verify citizenship status. With their help, we can ensure the most secure election in California history,” the justice department said. Bonta, the California attorney general, has raised questions about the evidence behind the suspected noncitizen ballots. “All they provided was a list of people and nothing about why they’re purportedly ineligible. If they have such information, we would be happy to review it, but they’ve provided none,” Bonta said at a recent press conference. The DoJ also charged 28 foreign nationals recently, accusing them of fraudulently registering to vote. “Today’s arrests prove what we have been saying,” Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney, said in a statement. “California is mailing ballots to noncitizens, and they are refusing to comply with federal law, which makes it a crime for noncitizens to vote. The voting rights of American citizens must be protected.” The defendants are lawful permanent residents, who have legal status in the US but are not citizens authorized to vote. Some state officials took no action on Friday’s letters, citing the fast-approaching election, which spurred a legal battle with the justice department. An appeals court is set to hear the matter on Tuesday. item.title: 12 people shot, including children, after Florida A&M homecoming game
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
At least 12 people, half of them juveniles and the youngest just 11 years old, were injured in a mass shooting near FAMU’s Bragg Memorial Stadium Saturday night amid homecoming weekend. Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said 11 people suffered gunshot wounds. Three victims were seriously injured, including one in critical condition, while eight were stable. A FAMU student was among the injured. Police said preliminary information indicates an altercation occurred between individuals before the shooting, which Revell called an "isolated incident." The latest: FAMU homecoming ends with one of city's worst mass shootings; six victims still hospitalized Midnight update: At least 12 injured in Perry Street shooting; youngest victim is 11 At least 12 people were injured, including six juveniles, in the shooting near FAMU’s Bragg Memorial Stadium Saturday night, Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said at a late-night press conference. “I stand before you tonight devastated,” Revell said. Eleven of the victims suffered gunshot wounds. Six victims are adults and six are juveniles, with the youngest just 11 years old, Revell said. A twelfth victim is the grandmother of one of the victims who was injured fleeing from the scene. He said one of the victims is a FAMU student. Three victims suffered serious injuries and one was in critical condition. Eight were in stable condition. He spoke directly to the victims and their families: "We hurt with you, and we will continue to get you the answers you so desperately want." The shooting occurred just before 8 p.m. near Perry and Manatee streets. Preliminary information indicates an altercation occurred between individuals before the shooting, Revell said. No one has been arrested at this time. Revell said investigators believe this was an "isolated incident between two or three individuals and nothing more than that." He asked anyone who saw anything or knows anything to come forward with information. Anyone with information is asked to call TPD at 850-891-4200 or Crime Solvers at 850-574-TIPS. More information will be released as it becomes available. "My message to the community is this... No family should have to experience this kind of violence, this kind of fear, this kind of heartbreak," he said. Revell took a moment to recognize "some of the heroic efforts" of first responders. "We had officers who were picking up victims and carrying them in their arms to transport because they couldn't get through the mass of people," he said. While choking up, he said it's critical for crowds to disperse so officers can get to victims. "Without hesitation they ran into the middle of this, still not knowing where the shooters were, still not knowing how many victims they had. They ran into the middle of this and put themselves in harms way." After midnight, Tallahassee Mayor John Dailey posted on x that “this is a truly horrific and heartbreaking tragedy.” “Tonight and in the days ahead, the FAMU family is not alone,” he wrote. “Our entire community stands with you.” 11:22 p.m. TPD and FAMU to hold press conference The Tallahassee Police Department and Florida A&M University Police Department will hold a press conference at 11:30 p.m. Saturday to provide updates on the Perry Street incident. The briefing will be held on FAMU’s campus at 1845 Althea Gibson Way. The announcement comes as authorities continue investigating the shooting near Bragg Memorial Stadium. Police previously said there were victims, but the number of people injured and the extent of their injuries remained unknown. The Tallahassee Democrat livestreamed it here. 11:10 p.m. FAMU issues statement: 'Our hearts go out to the victims and all those affected' At about 11 p.m., Florida A&M University issued a statement on the shooting through a Sachs Media representative sharing its condolences and saying the "campus remains safe." “The University is aware of an incident that occurred near campus on Perry Street on the evening of October 24. The Tallahassee Police Department is on the scene and actively investigating the situation." “Our hearts go out to the victims and all those affected by this tragic incident. While the campus remains safe, individuals are encouraged to avoid the area to allow law enforcement to conduct its investigation." “The safety and security of our students, faculty, and staff remain our highest priority. We are closely monitoring the situation and will share additional updates as more information becomes available. Anyone who has information about the situation is encouraged to contact the Tallahassee Police Department.” Anyone with information is asked to call TPD at 850-891-4200 or Crime Solvers at 850-574-TIPS. More information will be released as it becomes available. 10:30 p.m.: Social media videos show scenes of chaos Video of the shooting and its aftermath are circulating on social media. One video viewed by tens of thousands of people on Facebook shows police carrying a victim through a parking lot on a cloth stretcher. Another shows officers giving medical attention to a person on the ground by flashlight as people shout all around. Still another shows a swarm of police in all directions managing a crowd of bystanders. Trash litters the scene from where people fled in panic as bystanders talk about someone being hit in the head and another being shot in the back. "Everybody ran; everybody cleared off," a person can be heard saying. People also began coming to grips with the magnitude of the shooting on social media. "I can only imagine the level of panic and chaos that an incident of this magnitude may have caused. Beyond those directly affected by the shooting, my concern is that hundreds, perhaps even thousands, of people may have rushed to safety, potentially creating dangerous crowd surges and resulting in additional injuries," a pastor wrote on FAMU's Facebook page. "I sincerely pray that the number of injuries is minimal and that everyone affected is safe." ▶ Did you witness the shooting or its aftermath? Share your stories, photos or videos with us at news@tallahassee.com . Others took to social media to say their friends, family and loved ones were safe. "Praying for our kids because what I just witnessed at 7:50pm was unbelievable. My 1st and last homecoming. On God! My kids and their friends were crying and I'm trying to pull other people kids to safety," a witness wrote on Facebook. "This could have been any of our babies." A video taken earlier in the day before the gunfire showed massive crowds walking along Perry Street amid the homecoming festivities. 10:05 p.m. update: FSU issues alert to students: 'As a precaution,' stay indoors At 10 p.m., Florida State University issued an "Emergency Message for the Florida State University Tallahassee Campus" with the extraordinary advice to avoid going outside on a weekend evening. "Florida State University is aware of reports of an off-campus shooting near Bragg Stadium on the FAMU campus in Tallahassee earlier this evening (Sat. Oct 24). At this time, there is no indication that members of the FSU community were involved. As a precaution, students, faculty and staff in the Tallahassee area are advised to remain indoors this evening and stay alert. The university will provide additional information as appropriate." This is an Emergency Message for the Florida State University Tallahassee Campus. Florida State University is aware of reports of an off-campus shooting near Bragg Stadium on the FAMU campus in Tallahassee earlier this evening (Sat. Oct 24). At this t https://t.co/M1KzwIWsgV — FSU Alert (@FSUAlert) October 25, 2026 10 p.m.: TPD says scene is secure; no word on victims Alicia Hill with the Tallahassee Police Department told the Tallahassee Democrat at 9:45 p.m. that the scene was secure. She had not additional information about the number of victims or extent of injuries. She also could not say specifically where the gunfire occurred on Perry Street. TPD's online crime tracking map notes an 8:02 p.m. call to "Assist Other Agencies" at Perry and Manatee Streets, which is an intersection next to Bragg Stadium. FAMU posted at about 10 p.m. "TPD is investigating a shooting on Perry Street. The number of victims and extent of injuries are unknown. Please avoid the area while officers investigate." 9:15 p.m. UPDATE: TPD reports shooting on Perry Street with victims after FAMU issues 'shelter in place alert' The Tallahassee Police Department (TPD) posted on social media that it "is currently investigating a shooting on Perry Street. At this time, the number of victims and the extent of their injuries are unknown." "Community members are encouraged to avoid the area while officers conduct their investigation," the post on social media said. The news broke during a busy Florida A&M homecoming weekend and shortly after the Rattlers lost their homecoming game to Arkansas-Pine Bluff. The university sent out a campus safety alert at 8:40 p.m. to "shelter in place" and avoid the area near Bragg Stadium. TPD spokesperson Alicia Hill was heading to the scene but had no additional information other than to say "there certainly are victims." Hill said TPD was closing down Perry Street, and she said the agency would provide more updates when information was available. As news of the shooting spread, people who were on Perry Street began to post on social media what they saw. "Perry St was wild tonight. Running, falling, ducking and hiding," one person wrote. "They literally just shot these ppl in front of me," another person wrote. "Yall please pray for they families." A Tallahassee Democrat photojournalist said she heard a lot of sirens coming from multiple directions at about 8:15 p.m. She heard fire engines heading over probably 7-10 minutes later, and flying above were multiple police drones overhead headed toward Bragg. ORIGINAL STORY Florida A&M University issued a public safety alert Saturday night warning people to avoid the area around Bragg Memorial Stadium because of police activity. “FAMU Alert: Police activity near Bragg Stadium and perry street. Avoid the area or shelter in place if nearby,” the university said in the social media alert. The alert was posted at about 8:40 p.m., shortly after FAMU’s homecoming football loss. FAMU Alert: Police activity near Bragg Stadium and perry street . A Tallahassee Police Department Watch commander was not immediately available. People near Bragg Stadium and Perry Street were advised either to avoid the area or shelter in place. item.title: Trump announces $4 billion Audi factory in Georgia ahead of midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Bo Erickson and David Shepardson PERRY, Georgia, Oct 25 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that Audi plans to build a $4 billion assembly plant in Georgia that will produce 200,000 SUVs annually, as he seeks to convince Americans to back Republicans in the November midterm elections. Trump, who has pressured automakers ‌to move production to the United States and has raised tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum and parts, made the announcement at a rally in Perry, near Macon in ‌central Georgia, where Volkswagen's premium subsidiary intends to build its first US assembly plant. Last year, Trump's tariffs dealt Audi a €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion) blow as it imports all its vehicles for the US market from Europe or Mexico. Georgia has ​competitive election races for US Senate and governor and Trump is eager to make the case that his auto tariffs are helping the US economy. Critics say they have boosted vehicle prices and that the trade uncertainty has delayed some automaker investments. "We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia," Audi CEO Gernot Doellner said at the event. "This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market." In Germany, meanwhile, there has been increasing tension between Volkswagen management and workers over massive job cuts in the carmaker's home market, including ‌possible plant closures in light of rising costs and stiff Asian ⁠competition. "It is right and necessary to better tap into the US market via a new plant," said Christiane Benner, head of the IG Metall union and Volkswagen's deputy supervisory board chair. "However, firm prospects for workers at all sites, particularly those here in Germany, must be clearly defined and set ⁠out." She said a final decision on the investment would have to be taken by Volkswagen's supervisory board. Olaf Lies, state premier of the German state of Lower Saxony, Volkswagen's second-largest shareholder, said that expanded production in the US was an opportunity provided German workers also benefit. "Growth in America must secure jobs and value creation here and must not displace them," he said. REPUBLICAN SAYS TARIFFS BROUGHT AUDI PLANT TO UNITED STATES Audi said ​the ​investment will create approximately 4,500 jobs. Construction is scheduled to begin next year, with production starting in the ​early 2030s, Audi said. The plant is expected to assemble the Audi Q7, ‌Q8 and Q9 SUVs, a US official told Reuters. Audi also plans to build 25,000 vehicles a year in neighboring South Carolina, the official said. Some of the vehicles, now built in Europe, would be exported, the official added. Those vehicles will be assembled at a $2 billion plant of VW's off-road brand Scout Motors that is under construction in Blythewood, near the state capital, Columbia, the official said. "We regard the region as a key market for profitable growth," Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume said. "A potential Audi plant in the US would create further conditions for this." Trump has cut government incentives for electric vehicles, causing a significant reduction in EV and battery production in the country. US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year. A gold ‌Audi with manufacturer license plates was parked outside Trump's rally. US Senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, said ​late on Saturday that "with this investment, Audi will build all of their SUVs exclusively in the US". He said ​the Audi plant "would never have happened without tariffs, without common sense regulations and without ​eliminating California’s ability to regulate fuel economy standards". Audi sales have fallen for two consecutive years and slid 7% in the first half of 2026 as ‌fierce competition in China and US tariffs hit demand. Audi's US sales ​are down 16% this year. Audi's Neckarsulm plant in ​southwest Germany is one of four German Volkswagen plants facing possible closure after 2030. In July, Japan's Toyota said it would spend $3.6 billion to build a 2.5 million square foot (232,000 square metre) truck assembly line on its manufacturing campus in San Antonio, Texas, and shift some truck production to the US from Mexico. The Japanese automaker said the ​expansion would be completed by 2030, creating 2,000 jobs. Honda Motor is ‌considering building a US assembly plant but has warned it may not unless the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement on trade is extended. South Korea's Hyundai said last year that ​if it had certainty about USMCA, it "would immediately unlock over $20 billion in new American investments". (Reporting by Bo Erickson in Perry and David Shepardson in Washington; Additional ​reporting by Christoph Steitz and Rachel More; Editing by Nia Williams, Rod Nickel and David Goodman) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://finance.yahoo.com/news/trump-set-announce-plan-audi-213133434.html

item.title: About 1,300 clergy abuse survivors approve $800 million deal with New York archdiocese
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Archdiocese of New York and attorneys for about 1,300 parishioners who said they were sexually abused by clergy have agreed to an $800 million settlement of their legal claims, the second-largest involving a Catholic archdiocese in the U.S. Archbishop Ronald Hicks sent an email Saturday to clergy confirming the settlement after attorneys for the survivors of alleged abuse announced it. Hicks said the agreement will not be final until the parties sign it, an action scheduled for the week of Nov. 6. The only larger settlement over sexual abuse claims in the U.S. was by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, which agreed in 2024 to pay $880 million to 1,000 abuse victims, in addition to $740 million in claims it had paid previously. In June, the Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed to a $395 million settlement over about 500 lawsuits filed over clergy abuse, and in December 2025, a federal judge approved a settlement in which the Archdiocese of New Orleans agreed to pay at least $230 million to abuse victims. The agreement with the New York archdiocese would end more than seven years of lawsuits. The parties agreed to a framework for an agreement in May that required everyone who filed a claim to sign off. “The unanimous agreement of survivors who filed claims against the Archdiocese of New York marks a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice,” Jeff Anderson, an attorney representing people who filed more than 1,000 of claims against the Catholic Church in New York state, said in a statement. “Through their courage, sacrifice, and determination, survivors have helped bring about a reckoning and a meaningful step toward accountability.” The Archiocese of New York covers the city's boroughs of the Bronx, Manhattan and Staten Island as well as seven counties to the north of New York City and is home to about 300 churches, more than 150 parochial schools and 2.5 million Catholics. In his email to clergy, Hicks said that if church members ask about the settlement, “please let them know that much progress has been made.” “We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors,” he wrote. “This agreement will also allow the archdiocese to turn its full attention once again to its mission of preaching the Gospel, healing the sick, caring for the poor and needy, welcoming the stranger, and educating our children.” A New York law enacted in 2019 allows survivors of child sexual abuse to file lawsuits against their abusers and institutions that shielded them until they turn 55. People who had already had turned 55 when the law was enacted also were given until August 2021 to file lawsuits, no matter when the alleged abuse occurred. “This is an extraordinary achievement for the survivors,” said Trusha Goffe, an attorney in Anderson’s firm. "The survivors remined resolute through years of litigation to reach this monumental settlement.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/yorks-archdiocese-survivors-clergy-abuse-233516942.html
